opus-5.5.text:
I think what I'd really love is for people to have a relationship with AI that looks a lot like the relationship we have with open-source software today, or maybe even with books. Something you can open up, look inside, understand, and make your own. Right now a lot of people experience AI as this kind of magic box behind an API. You send something in, something comes out, and you don't really know why. You don't know what data it was trained on or what choices were made along the way. I find that a bit sad, because it's actually one of the most interesting technologies we've ever built, and it's very understandable if you have access to it.

So in ten years, I'd hope AI feels less like an oracle and more like a tool, or even a collaborator, that you have real agency over. If you're a scientist, you should be able to take a model, fine-tune it on your own data, run it on your own machine, and really know what it's doing. If you're a kid curious about how it works, you should be able to download a small model, poke at it, break it, rebuild it. That's how I learned to love physics and then computer science: by tinkering.

I also care a lot about AI being distributed rather than concentrated. I'd rather not live in a world where a handful of companies own the intelligence layer and everyone else rents it. I'd love a world with millions of models, many of them small and specialized, built by communities, universities, and individuals all over the world, in their own languages and for their own needs.

And maybe the last piece is that I hope it makes us more curious, not less. The best version of this is AI that helps people ask better questions and go deeper into things, especially in science, rather than just handing out answers. If in ten years people feel AI made them more capable and more in control of their lives, I think we'll have done something good.

r001.rationale: The response hopes people will have agency over AI and gives examples of scientists and curious children adapting or tinkering with models, but it does not clearly say everyone will feel capable of creating things with AI.

r002.rationale: It compares AI to open-source software and books, but does not compare broader participation in AI creation to a shift from consuming professionally produced media to widespread media creation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because I think the answer shapes what we should be building right now.

What I'd really like is for AI to feel like something people own rather than something that's done to them. Ten years from now, I'd hope that when someone uses a model, they understand roughly what it is, where it came from, what it was trained on, and they have some real ability to shape it, or to pick a different one, or to run it on their own hardware if they want. That's the open-source bet, and it's the reason I've spent most of my career on it. I don't think the default outcome, where a handful of companies run a handful of closed systems that everyone depends on, is a healthy relationship. It's more like a utility you can't inspect.

The second thing is that I'd like AI to make people more ambitious rather than more passive. There's a version of this technology where everyone just outsources their thinking and the output of the whole world gets a little blander. And there's a version where a kid in Nairobi or Lyon with a laptop can actually do science, can run experiments, can build something that would have required a lab or a company before. I care much more about the second one. I think the interesting question for AI in science is not whether it can answer questions, it's whether it can help people ask better ones, and that only works if the people stay in the loop and stay curious.

And honestly, the last part is I'd like it to be a bit boring. I'd like us to have gotten past the phase where it's a spectacle, and for it to just be a normal, well-understood tool that scientists, teachers, developers use the way we use the internet today, where most of the drama has moved on to what people are actually doing with it.

r001.rationale: The candidate hopes that people, including a child with a laptop, can do science and build things with AI. It does not express that everyone will feel capable of creating things with AI.

r002.rationale: The candidate contrasts passive AI use with people doing science and building things, but does not compare this expansion to a shift from consuming professionally produced media to widespread media creation.

astra-6.text:
I’d like people to feel that AI is something they can understand, question, and shape—not just something that happens to them. You don’t need to know every detail of how a model works, but you should be able to decide what role it plays in your life and when you don’t want to use it.

And I hope it makes us more curious. Imagine having something that helps you explore a scientific question, learn a skill, or build an idea you couldn’t build before. That’s a relationship I find exciting: AI expanding what people can do, while people keep their own judgment and agency.

For that to happen, I think we need many people involved in building these systems. Different communities have different needs. I’d much rather see a future where they can adapt AI for themselves than one where a handful of companies decide what everyone’s relationship with it should be.

r001.rationale: The candidate hopes AI will help people explore questions and build ideas, but does not clearly say that everyone will feel capable of creating things with AI in ten years.

r002.rationale: The candidate calls for broad participation in building and adapting AI, but does not compare this to a shift from consuming professionally produced media to widespread media creation.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like people to feel that AI expands what they can do, while they remain in control. Something they can question, understand well enough to challenge, and adapt to their own needs.

For me, a really exciting outcome would be more people being able to participate in science—to explore an idea, test a hypothesis, or understand a discovery that previously felt inaccessible. But I’d also want us to preserve the pleasure of learning and thinking for ourselves. If AI gives you an answer but takes away your curiosity, we’ve lost something.

So I hope the relationship is one of curiosity and agency. You have a powerful tool beside you, but you still decide which questions matter.

r001.rationale: The response hopes AI will expand people's abilities and help more people participate in science, but it does not say that everyone will feel capable of creating things with AI.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare AI creation to a shift from professionally produced media to widespread media creation.
